children.text: Saint Gregory the Great Parish Church in Majayjay was built in stone between 1616 and 1649 and completed in 1730, making it one of Laguna's finest Spanish-era churches. It became a National Cultural Treasure in 2001 and a minor basilica in January 2025, and it pairs well with nearby waterfalls and an unfinished bridge for a day trip.
Majayjay is a highland town at the far southeastern edge of Laguna, bordering Lucban in Quezon Province. It lies at the foot of Mount Banahaw, a mountain revered as sacred, about
107km

from Manila in a straight line. With a population of about 28,000 in the 2024 census, it is small, but its cool climate made it a favorite retreat from the Spanish era onward, and it is said to have served as a summer capital for colonial rulers before Baguio was developed. The building that stands at the heart of town is the Saint Gregory the Great Parish Church, commonly called Majayjay Church.

The church's history reaches back to the 16th century. In 1571 the Franciscans established a mission town here, and in 1575 residents built a first church near the May-it River, which burned the following year. In 1578 the priests Juan de Plasencia and Diego Oropesa built a nipa-and-bamboo church dedicated to Saint Gregory the Great, and in 1594 Antonio Nombela arrived as the first parish priest. A stone church was approved in 1599, but the makeshift church burned again in 1606, and the main stone construction ran from 1616 to 1649. After a partial fire in 1660, reconstruction from 1711 to 1730 gave the church its present form. Wikipedia records that at completion it was the largest church in the Philippines.

Trials continued afterward. About a century later a typhoon destroyed the stone structure, which was repaired in 1839, 1842 and 1848, and in 1892 the roof was replaced with galvanized iron. During the American occupation the church served as an army headquarters, war damage was repaired in 1912, and in 1954 it entered a government rehabilitation program with the National Conservation Society of the Philippines. In recognition of this value, a National Historical Commission marker was installed in 1993, and in 2001 the National Museum designated it a National Cultural Treasure (Level 1). On January 25, 2025, Pope Francis granted it minor basilica status, making it the first basilica in the Diocese of San Pablo.
The
Laguna pilgrimage guide

lists the church as the Minor Basilica and Parish of Saint Gregory the Great. See the stone façade and bell tower in central Majayjay, and ask the parish office about the interior and any displays in the adjoining convent. Check return transport in advance if continuing to waterfalls or outlying villages.
The church is about
long,
wide and
high. It is built of volcanic tuff, lumber and iron sheeting, and its walls are about
3m

thick, because the burned ruins were sandwiched between two layers of brick when it was rebuilt. The façade has three levels and ends in a triangular pediment with a round window. Wikipedia describes the style as Romanesque in its text but classifies it as Baroque in its infobox, so it is more accurate not to pin it to a single style.

The five-story bell tower has a conical roof and balustraded windows, and a large antique bell hangs in the belfry. It is visible from anywhere in town, so if you get lost, simply walk toward the tower. Ask the church office whether visitors may enter the tower.

Inside are the main altarpiece (retablo mayor), four smaller altarpieces, azulejo tile floors, antique saints, reliquaries and liturgical objects. Worshippers take priority during Mass, so take photos quietly at times when no service is under way. Dress that covers shoulders and knees is the polite choice.

The convent beside the church is described as one of the best-preserved Spanish-era convents in the country and the earliest surviving example of its kind. Inside is a small museum of old parish documents and ecclesiastical silver, and part of the building is used by the Catholic school Liceo de Majayjay. Museum hours may not be fixed.

blocks.title: Chapel of Nuestra Señora de la Porteria (Ermita)

children.text: The Ermita chapel in the Origuel area was built as a tribunal in the Spanish period and later became a chapel. Its image of the Virgin is said to have arrived in Majayjay in 1759 and to have been enshrined in 1760. It is close to the main church, so the two are easy to see together.

This unfinished 19th-century bridge over the Pagsanjan River links Majayjay and Magdalena. It is said to be most impressive viewed from below, and Wikivoyage notes that the main access trail is overgrown and passes a dumpsite, so it suggests entering from the Majayjay–Magdalena Road instead. Approach carefully, especially right after rain, when it is slippery.
The most visited waterfall in Majayjay is about

high. It is also called Imelda Falls because former First Lady Imelda Marcos financed tourism promotion there. In typhoons or heavy rain the current can become dangerous and the falls may be closed, and after rain the water can turn muddy, so check the weather before you go.
Dalitiwan Stream is known for cold water coming down from Mount Banahaw, and two nearby resorts provide access to cascades and rock pools. Sprite Falls is about
15 minutes
on foot from the Piit barangay hall, and Bukal Falls (Kilangin Falls) requires a hike of about
30–40 minutes
from the barangay hall.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: Church and waterfall in one day

children.text: Leave Manila and head to Majayjay by way of southern Laguna. The mountain road is winding and the trip is long, so an early start is necessary.
Arrive in Majayjay town and tour the church on F. Blumentritt Street. Take your time over the bell tower, the façade, and the interior altars and tile floor.
Browse souvenirs at the church office and ask whether the convent museum next door is open.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town or near the market.
Visit Taytay Falls and cool off by the water. If it has rained heavily, ask a guard or a local about conditions first.
See the Ermita chapel or the Puente del Capricho, and arrange a ride back before dark.
Public transport is infrequent, so it is hard to find a ride back late in the afternoon. Plan to leave Majayjay by 4 PM at the latest.

items.title: Two-day highland town route
items.subtitle: Linking Majayjay with Lucban and Liliw

children.text: See the church and the Ermita chapel, and walk around town.
Visit one or two waterfalls and stay overnight in town. Wikivoyage lists Hilarion's Farm and La Triccias Resort as lodging options; check rates locally.
Head east toward Lucban or Luisiana, or go west via Liliw toward San Pablo.
Take a bus from Buendia or PITX to Santa Cruz in Laguna, then a jeepney to Majayjay. The
Santa Cruz terminal directory
lists
one way for the jeepney.
Majayjay town is about
by road from Santa Cruz. Allow time for the jeepney to fill.
A private car or rental car is the most convenient. The two-lane mountain highways are winding, and some secondary roads are in fair to poor condition.
Exact bus routes and fares change, so check before you leave.
Jeepneys to Lucban, Luisiana, Santa Cruz and Nagcarlan leave from the Majayjay Transport Cooperative terminal on Ordoñez Street.
Jeepneys depart when full, and waiting in Magdalena for a Majayjay jeepney can take up to about
1 hour
You can transfer to San Pablo via Liliw to the west.
Tricycles are the main transport between barangays.
For Taytay Falls, use the registration area in Barangay Gagalot. The
waterfall visitor guide
allows about
10–20 minutes
on foot. Check access first after heavy rain.
Majayjay is a highland town and cooler than the lowlands. Average temperatures are about
in January and about
in May. The dry season is better for both the church and the waterfalls.
In the rainy season the waterfalls often turn rough, close, or run muddy. If you only want to see the church, a rainy-season visit is possible, but check mountain road conditions in advance.

Majayjay is a small town with limited lodging and dining. The lodging Wikivoyage lists is Hilarion's Farm on the Majayjay–Lucban Road and La Triccias Resort Hotel in Piit. We could not confirm rates, so contact them directly before booking.

For food, use the market or restaurants in town. There is a convenience store on Blumentritt Street and a public market on Balagtas Street. If you continue to nearby Lucban, you can also try local specialties, so add it if your schedule allows.
For a day trip, check the last return jeepney and pickup point when you arrive. Service can be sparse later in the day.
Respect worshippers' prayer time inside the church, and refrain from taking photos during Mass.
Wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.
The waterfalls are dangerous after heavy rain. Ask a local about conditions first.
The known trail to the Puente del Capricho is rough, so enter from the Majayjay–Magdalena Road.
Wikivoyage lists the Majayjay Tourism, History, Culture, and Arts Office (+63 917 548 0086) for inquiries. The number may change.
Now that it is a minor basilica, pilgrim numbers may rise, so expect crowds on weekends and feast days.
Bring plenty of cash. ATMs may be absent or scarce in a small town.
Mountain roads and waterfalls are strongly affected by weather. Postpone your visit during typhoons or heavy rain.
Jeepneys are infrequent, so it is hard to find a ride back if you leave late.
Riding on top of a jeepney is illegal and dangerous.
Waterfalls can be closed because of dangerous torrents after heavy rain.
Church hours and museum opening days can change, so check the latest announcements.
Trails near the unfinished bridge may be poorly maintained.
A slipper town that continues to the west and can be reached from Majayjay. You transfer jeepneys; check travel times locally.
Jeepneys to Nagcarlan leave from the Majayjay terminal. It is a Spanish-era site in Laguna that pairs well with the church visit.
Twin volcanic lakes on the Nagcarlan side that you can add to a Laguna highland route.
A neighboring town in Quezon Province, about
12km
from Majayjay.
